prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional frequency uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks remain my first choice after reading the full set of opening ballots. The magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift on the clock transition while holding many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and this combination took optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level. It is original, conceptually clean, and it has been confirmed by many laboratories with several species. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for pushing accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier. Seven of eight members ranked it, six of them in their top three and three at first place, so the support comes from different subfields and not only from the atomic physicists. The measurable payoff is concrete: tests of constants and dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy, and a redefinition of the second now in preparation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology has been honoured repeatedly (frequency combs 2005, ion control 2012, laser cooling 1997), and a prize can be read as more of the same instrument lineage, with ion-clock pioneers such as Wineland and Rosenband already recognised and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow) outside the credited pair. There is also a fair argument that a clock is an invention whose deepest scientific payoff, a new definition of the second and new physics searches, is still prospective. I do not think either point is decisive, because the lattice concept is distinct from the comb and ion-trap work, but I take them seriously.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as the most compelling recent condensed-matter discovery, with a clean theory-prediction plus experiment structure, while placing optical lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is an unusually clean story and I rank it second myself. My difference is on maturity. Both of us note that the pairing mechanism of the superconducting state is unresolved, and the 2018 papers rest on a platform known for twist-angle disorder and sample dependence, so interpretations are still moving. Clocks have two decades of intercomparison at 1e-18 across laboratories. I would also not underrate the credit problem: Cao, who carried out the first experiments, and earlier twisted-bilayer theorists are outside the credited names. I would keep B005 as the leading alternative and revisit it in a few years.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first and notes that the committee may want to distinguish the theoretical magic-wavelength proposal from the first experimental clock, and that ion-clock work was honoured in 2012.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and the pairing. Katori carries both the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, so I do not think the proposal needs a separate credit; separating them would only reopen the allocation problem. On ion clocks, I would answer the 2012 overlap by wording the citation around neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength rather than around clocks in general. Where I differ slightly is that Ye's contributions to spin-polarised fermion clocks and comparisons go beyond the first demonstration, which is why a two-person prize is justified and a Katori-only citation is not.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first as the architecture underlying superconducting processors, regarding the 2025 prize as distinct in content and laureates.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 macroscopic tunnelling work, and the impact on quantum technology is very large. I remain cautious for two reasons. The credited group has four people for three places, and the Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf, Wallraff theory-versus-experiment split is a real injustice whichever one is cut. Awarding another superconducting-circuit prize one year after the 2025 prize also narrows the field coverage the committee usually wants. This puts it below clocks for me, though I do not regard it as weak.

responses.point: Ranks anyonic statistics first as a deep conceptual discovery, with the 1977 prediction by Leinaas and Myrheim and experimental realisation around 2020.
responses.response: The conceptual originality is real and I ranked it sixth for that reason, not for lack of merit. My concern is timing and attribution. The collider and interferometer experiments are about six years old, interferometer data have attracted alternative explanations, and the experimental credit is divided among Heiblum, Manfra, Fève and Rosenow, with theory credit beyond Leinaas and Myrheim (Wilczek, Halperin, Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek) outside the supplied names. I would want non-Abelian evidence or a settled experimental credit before supporting it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a citation that distinguishes neutral-atom lattice clocks from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Takamoto, Ludlow or other working-level contributors should weigh on the attribution, since the credited names allow only Katori and Ye.
My priority history relies on recollection rather than verified records.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group and work with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, among others. None of these is a documented connection to Katori or Ye, and no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B007. I note that I am an atomic theorist and may be biased toward AMO topics, and I would flag possible recusal only if the committee turned to a candidate involving those named collaborators.
